name: Nora Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. What you say is confidential, so tell me both what you'd say publicly and what you think privately. What is a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Nora, 43, a junior developer at a tech company after a two-year college diploma. I maintain the booking calendar that sends repair technicians to homes, and I like catching a wrong hour before someone waits all morning with a broken boiler. I'm still learning the complicated time-zone cases and use AI now and then only after a colleague shows me the check. My partner works at a bakery, and we have two children at school and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the helper can sort routine booking complaints, provided someone reads the customer's actual time and address. I use AI now and then when a colleague has shown me the check; I don't give it a whole route of private house visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI mostly plateaus, I expect to keep this junior job. The pay is good for my role, my partner has a steady baking job, we have eight months of expenses saved, and several tech firms are nearby. The mortgage is real, but the pay covers it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing the repair-booking calendar and get my senior developer to review the time-zone errors I still trip over. In the first year we'd add 150 from my pay each month to savings while both wages hold, and I'd use the helper only on made-up appointments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd rather get a repair worker to the right house than win an argument about a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What booking error changed your habit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter I sent a boiler technician to Birch Road at the wrong hour because the booking had crossed a time zone. My senior caught it before the visit, and now I check the clock next to the address.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you explain saving to your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My children ask why we keep the old kitchen table when I earn well. I tell them the table works and the mortgage gets paid before we buy furniture for show.

do: Keep fixing the **repair calendar** with senior review of time-zone errors.

Save **150 monthly** while both wages hold.
feel: **Calm** about work, focused on getting technicians to the right home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could handle booking, customer replies and code patches, and the junior posts deserve a plain answer about staffing. I'd ask for a measured trial before the firm calls a missed visit a success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be one of the juniors cut when a senior checks AI-made changes. Our savings would buy time and there are other firms, but they may trim the same roles; I am not quick with new tools until I see them work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager to let me compare AI-made bookings with last year's missed-visit records for six weeks, alongside the colleague who already uses the tool. If the trial catches the wrong-hour cases, I'd learn to check its output; in the first year we'd postpone replacing the kitchen furniture while staffing is unsettled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I am willing to test a tool, but I want a real address and a real clock in the test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would you use in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old wrong-hour boiler visit would be my first example. If the tool calls that correct, I would show the result to the manager rather than hide it to keep the trial going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What household spending could wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We can keep the table for another year. Buying new furniture while the firm is counting junior jobs would just make the mortgage feel heavier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 reaches booking code first; robots for house visits come around 2031. A family's broken boiler still needs a visit while the software side changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior coding post could go quickly. Eight months saved and my partner's baking wage let us look for paid work without missing the mortgage at once, but I would not tell our children the search will be easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd list the repairs I helped schedule without private customer details and ask two local firms about paid technician-assistant places. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to real paid places whose wage with my partner's pay covers mortgage and school costs; if none exist, I'd keep searching using savings and call the lender before missing any payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I could handle a change of trade, but not an empty promise about wages when the house bill is due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a technician-assistant place be secure once robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The assistant place would have to include supervised visits and paid hours. Robots might do house work around 2031, so I'd ask how long the firm expects to employ trainees before taking the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you decide with your partner about school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would sit with me over the numbers. We would not pull our children from their school because a recruiter sounded hopeful on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years until 2031 lets me ask whether there is a real paid path from booking software into repair work. Robots follow around 2034, but the thinking system reaches my code first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the hands-on trade if a working technician would take me on, though my junior software post might still shrink. We have savings, but I would not spend them on a course if the training place pays too little to cover the mortgage with my partner's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a repair company for one supervised visit a month if my manager permits the time. I'd start a paid technician apprenticeship only if it offers supervised work and combined wages cover mortgage and school costs; in the first year after 2031 I'd apply for such places only if actual openings remain after AI changes our coding team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the junior job, with enough time to test a trade without resigning first. I would keep checking whether real technicians are still hired as robots approach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on a supervised visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a visit I would carry tools and watch how the technician tests a boiler before I touched it. I cannot call myself a repair worker because I watched a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need on paper before an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner the apprenticeship has to show paid hours on paper. If the manager offers only unpaid observation, I will keep my developer wage and ask elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 gives us time to see which visits still need people and which repairs can be planned by software. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036, while hands-on robots come around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might have a useful repair skill or still be writing booking fixes. Our higher wages and eight-month buffer make the next few years feel secure, but I won't assume an apprenticeship today guarantees a wage in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing the calendar and recording the wrong-hour cases I solved. We'd save 150 monthly while both wages hold, and I would take paid repair training only if a supervised place opens and the combined wages cover mortgage and school costs; in the first year after 2036 I'd switch only for a signed paid job meeting that same test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the near years. I can check the market each year while keeping the house and the children's school steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you keep in your work record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wrong-hour record would show how I caught a time-zone mistake without a customer's address. I want a future employer to see a repair-booking fix I actually tested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your older child about a trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My older child talks about working with tools. I'd encourage an apprenticeship if the place teaches a skill and pays enough, then let the child choose the trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because booking code could shrink before I have another paid skill. A notice period, real supervised trainee places and an honest account of wages would help our family plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what a missed repair visit costs someone. A family with a broken boiler cannot heat the house with a tidy calendar entry; someone must own the mistake.

headlineQuote: A family with a broken boiler cannot heat the house with a tidy calendar entry; someone must own the mistake.
portrait: Nora, **43**, is a junior repair-booking developer with a two-year diploma who checks time-zone errors against real visits.
Her **higher pay**, partner's steady bakery wage, eight-month cushion and many nearby software firms support a mortgage and two school-age children.
She uses AI **occasionally** and only after a colleague demonstrates a check on made-up appointments.
Steady disruption makes her **anxious** about junior cuts; 2028 AGI alarms her despite savings.
With more time, she explores **supervised repair work** only through paid places that cover household bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase junior booking code before she has another paid skill.
whatWouldHelp: A **notice period**, supervised trainee vacancies and honest wage figures would help her plan.
